To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the interfacial concentration profile develops according a general square root law; (ii) this law can be used to extract mutual diffusion coefficients of oriented mesophase; (iii) the evaporation of a complex solution is self-regulated by a humidity range that corresponds to the stability range of the lamellar phase.
the evaporation of water from complex aqueous solution leads to the build up of a concentration gradient at the interface with air.

the evaporation rate from a binary system composed of a surfactant and water, which is in a lamellar liquid crystalline state at the drying interface, follows a t-1/ 2 scaling law, and that this is due to diffusion in the liquid crystalline phase being slower than diffusion in the bulk liquid phase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the understanding of the mechanisms of water evaporation from aqueous solutions, which is of fundamental interest and has a large impact on many technological applications.
the study of water evaporation from complex solutions and the self-regulation of the process.
the study of the interfacial phenomena that occur at drying aqueous solutions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evaporation rate of complex aqueous solutions is determined by the transport properties of the mesophases that self-assemble at the air-liquid interface.
the interfacial gradients are the consequence of the interplay between the evaporation process and the self-assembly of the system.
the evaporation rate is controlled by a competition between diffusion of the different phases in the liquid phase and diffusion of water in the gas phase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evaporation rate from a drying complex solution depends on the mutual diffusion coefficients of the mesostructured phases that are present in the interfacial region.
the evaporation rate from complex solutions is controlled by diffusion in the liquid, which is a direct result of the formation of mesostructures at the interface.
we have developed a new experimental setup and theoretical framework for the quantitative description of evaporation and diffusion at complex drying interfaces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evaporation rate is not constant but decreases with time, and the interfacial structure is not static but develops according to a square root of time evolution law.
the interfacial structure and the mutual diffusion coefficients of the different phases are crucial to understand the dynamics of evaporation from aqueous solutions.
the self-assembly of complex aqueous solutions at drying interfaces can lead to the formation of a self-regulation layer that can significantly reduce water evaporation.
